description_full: Value Line, Inc. engages in the production and sale of investment periodicals and related publications. Its investment periodicals and related publications cover a range of investments, including stocks, mutual funds, exchange traded funds (ETFs), and options. The company offers comprehensive research services, including The Value Line Investment Survey - Small and Mid-Cap, The Value Line 600, and The Value Line Fund Advisor Plus that provide statistical and text coverage of various investment securities, with an emphasis placed on its proprietary research, analysis, and statistical ranks. It also provides niche newsletters comprising Value Line Select: Dividend Income & Growth, Value Line Select: ETFs, The Value Line Special Situations Service, The Value Line M&A Service, The Value Line Climate Change Investing Service, and The Value Line Information You Should Know Wealth Newsletter; digital versions of its products through its website, www.valueline.com; investment management services; The Value Line Research Center, which provides on-line access; and investment analysis software, such as The Value Line Investment Analyzer and The New Value Line ETFs Service. In addition, the company offers current and historical financial databases comprising financial DataFile, estimates and projections, and mutual funds; and copyright products, which include unit investment trusts, variable annuities, managed accounts, and ETFs. Further, it operates as publishing unit for investment related to periodical publications and copyrights; places advertising on behalf of the company's publications; and distributes print publications. It serves municipal and university libraries, corporations, colleges, individual investors, and investment management professionals. The company was founded in 1931 and is headquartered in New York, New York. Value Line, Inc. operates as a subsidiary of Arnold Bernhard & Co., Inc.

financial_summary: Value Line, Inc. is a small-cap financial services business with a $398M market cap on $33M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -6% over the past three years and -0% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $19M in free cash flow — roughly 56 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.86× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 92% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 12% operating margin trails the Financial Services median (29%) by 17pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.46x its revenue share).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 15% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.01 vs 5y 0.52), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $86K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 58% in the 2022 bear market and 48% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $24.91 (margin of safety -70%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.41 to $31.57 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/E 20.1 vs 12.2, EV/EBITDA 68.2 vs 10.9 and P/FCF 21.4 vs 12.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 124% above its 10-year median.
The price implies 8.7% annual cash-flow growth, 12pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.67).
It converts 56% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 20% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -5.5% over 3 years, -3.7% over 5 years and -0.3% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 6.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 92.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 6%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase).
It returns 3.3% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 3.3% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 8.7% a year over the last five.
people: With about 106 employees, each generates about $316K of revenue, 0.6x the Financial Services median.
